title: Tide and Bakery
premise: After a catastrophic final performance ends her orchestral career, cellist Wren Whitlock retreats to the coastal town of Saltmere to save her late aunt's failing bakery, whose lease expires in six months. A community pen-pal program meant to pair lonely strangers instead pairs Wren — anonymously — with Theo Marsh, the developer's son sent to buy out the bakery block, and neither realizes at first that their tender letters and their bitter real-life feud involve the same person. As the lease deadline looms, Wren must choose between the safe half-measures she's always lent her heart in and the whole-hearted risk of loving a man whose family is destroying everything she's rebuilding. In the end, Theo publicly breaks from his father's project, Wren performs again for the town that saved her, and together they re-open the bakery on new terms — love chosen over duty.
about_author: Jude Galloway is the pen name of a former pastry chef who traded early-morning ovens for late-night manuscripts after a decade of feeding a small seaside town. They write romances about second chances, stubborn buildings, and people who learn to play the whole song.

chapters.title: The Broken String
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Flashback to the concert where her hands failed mid-solo before two thousand people; she walks off stage and never returns. Present day: she arrives in Saltmere to inventory her aunt's crumbling bakery. Emotional beat: grief disguised as practicality, and the first hint that flour might forgive what music wouldn't.

chapters.title: Six Months of Flour
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She reads the lease: six months to make the bakery solvent or lose it to the Harrow Development Group. The townsfolk are skeptical of the outsider niece. Emotional beat: defiant commitment to a business she barely knows, masking terror of another public failure.

chapters.title: The Man Measuring Doorways
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Sent by his father to assess the bakery block for demolition, Theo measures doorframes while Wren glares. Their first exchange is acid and sparks. He lies about who he is — just 'a consultant.' Emotional beat: guilt he can't name yet, attraction he resents.

chapters.title: Anonymous Correspondents
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The town librarian strong-arms Wren into the Saltmere Pen-Pal Project to 'integrate.' She writes a guarded first letter venting about a man who measured her aunt's doorways like a vulture. Emotional beat: relief of honesty without a face attached.

chapters.title: Letters Signed with Initials
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. His assigned pen pal's letter about the doorway man lands like a slap; he answers honestly, confessing he may be complicit in something ugly. Neither signs a full name. Emotional beat: the strange intimacy of confessing to a stranger you're also deceiving in daylight.

chapters.title: Sourdough and Sabotage
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The bakery's first relaunch week: a health inspector arrives suspiciously fast after Theo's survey visit. Wren confronts him; he denies involvement but quietly fixes her broken oven at 2 a.m., unasked. Emotional beat: enemies discovering each other's competence and kindness against their will.

chapters.title: What the Tide Takes
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Walking the seawall, Theo writes his pen pal about his father's philosophy — buy, flatten, profit — and admits he's never chosen anything himself. Wren, reading it that night, feels seen in a way she hates needing. Emotional beat: parallel loneliness converging.

chapters.title: The Harvest Festival Disaster
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the festival, Wren's stall floods when a 'misplaced' drainage gate opens; Theo wades in to save her stock, and they laugh, soaked, for the first time. That night both write their pen pals about almost kissing someone they shouldn't. Emotional beat: the feud cracking open into want.

chapters.title: Half a Heart on Loan
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Theo asks her out properly; she agrees but keeps one foot out the door, still hiding the letters, still planning her exit if the bakery dies. Her cello sits untouched in the corner. Emotional beat: the old habit of lending pieces instead of risking the whole.

chapters.title: His Father's Blueprint
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Marcus Marsh unveils the full development plan at a town meeting — the bakery block first. Theo must sit silent beside him while Wren watches him from the crowd. Emotional beat: shame crystallizing; duty and desire now openly at war.

chapters.title: The Letter I Shouldn't Have Written
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Furious and hurt, Wren writes her anonymous pen pal a raw letter about betrayal by someone she was starting to love — naming no names but describing Theo exactly. Theo receives it and understands, with horror, that his pen pal is her. Emotional beat: dread and clarity arriving together.

chapters.title: Almost Confessions
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo tries twice to tell Wren the truth — as consultant, as son, as pen pal — and fails both times, retreating into a kiss instead. Wren senses the evasion. Emotional beat: intimacy built on a fault line, trembling.

chapters.title: Lease Expiration, Clause Nine
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds an old clause: the lease voids early if the building is condemned. An anonymous complaint triggers inspection. She suspects Theo's firm; he swears it wasn't him. For the first time, she doesn't believe him. Emotional beat: trust fracturing under pressure.

chapters.title: The Unmasking
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The librarian, tidying the pen-pal archive, lets slip handwriting details; Wren matches the letters to Theo's survey notes. She confronts him with both identities laid bare — the letters and the lie. Emotional beat: devastation that cuts both ways; he learns she knows everything at once.

chapters.title: Silence Between Movements
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Wren returns his letters unopened. Theo finally plays her a voicemail his father left — proof Marcus ordered the condemnation complaint — then goes home to confront Marcus and is disowned. Emotional beat: choosing integrity with nothing yet gained in return.

chapters.title: The Cello in the Corner
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Alone, Wren opens the returned letters and reads them all in one night, then picks up the cello for the first time in a year. Her hands shake; she keeps playing. Emotional beat: understanding that courage is the same muscle whether it holds a bow or a heart.

chapters.title: Condemned
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The inspection condemns the building; the lease collapses. Townsfolk rally with petitions and protest, but paperwork moves faster than love. Wren packs the ovens and refuses to cry in public. Emotional beat: rock bottom — the dream lost, the man unforgiven, pride all that's left.

chapters.title: What Theo Marsh Buys
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Using his inheritance and severance, Theo outbids his father's group at auction and buys the bakery block outright — then hands Wren the deed and the truth, asking nothing. She slams the door anyway. Emotional beat: sacrifice offered without guarantee, which is the only kind that counts.

chapters.title: The Whole Heart
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren realizes she's repeating her old pattern — punishing vulnerability instead of answering it. She writes Theo one final letter, unsigned no longer, and delivers it herself: every fear, every feeling, the whole heart at last. Emotional beat: the risk she's avoided since the concert stage.

chapters.title: Crescendo at the Seawall
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Climax: at the town's winter concert, Wren takes the stage in Saltmere for her first performance since the failure — playing while Theo, in the front row, publicly announces the bakery will reopen as a co-operative owned by the town. Marcus arrives to object and is turned away by neighbors. Emotional beat: triumph earned collectively; love and music reclaimed in the same breath.

chapters.title: First Batch, First Light
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reopening morning: flour dust in sunlight, Theo kneading badly, the town queued out the door. Wren pins the original lease to the wall framed — as history, not threat. Emotional beat: quiet joy; the second chance she never believed in, arrived on its own timing.

chapters.title: Tide and Bakery
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, epilogue. One year later: pen-pal night at the bakery, where strangers become friends over warm bread; Wren teaches a kids' cello class in the back room; Theo writes her a new letter even though they share a bed. Final image: the tide going out and coming back, always. Emotional beat: love as a practice, renewed daily.
